title: Ajahn Funn: Maṅsa-rogo: Muscles have their illnesses. They get sore and sprained. Nhāru-rogo: Tendons have their illnesses—what do you say to that? Everything can get…
content:
The Body Itself Is Made of Germs: Illness in Every Part

Maṅsa-rogo: Muscles have their illnesses. They get sore and sprained. Nhāru-rogo: Tendons have their illnesses—what do you say to that? Everything can get ill and malfunction. Aṭṭhi-rogo: Bones have their illnesses. Aṭṭhimiñja-rogo: Bone marrow has its illnesses.

So think about it. There are illnesses, there’s malfunctioning everywhere in the body. You can’t find a single part that doesn’t have its illnesses—simply that they haven’t come out of hiding and acted up. There’s illness down to every pore. The Buddha said that the body itself is made of germs.

This is what we get when we come to live in this world. That’s why the Buddha taught us to want to get out of the world, why he laid down the principles of generosity, virtue, and meditation, or virtue, concentration, and discernment. He taught the religion so that we could contemplate and see these four noble truths. When we see these four noble truths, we won’t be deluded by the world. We’ll be able to escape from it.

title: Ajahn Funn: Concerning this, the Buddha's quality of Dhamma is described as ehipassiko — calling all beings to come and see the Dhamma. He invites…
content:
Ehipassiko: Come and See Birth – See That Your Own Self Is the One Born

Concerning this, the Buddha's quality of Dhamma is described as ehipassiko — calling all beings to come and see the Dhamma. He invites us to see the Dhamma. Opanayiko — he invites us to bring it inward, to come and see. See birth. What is it that is born? This very self of ours is the one born. If we see that our own birth is suffering itself, we will let go on our own. If we do not see that our own self is suffering, we cannot let go. It is like lifting a heavy object. If we realize it is heavy, then we put it down. If we do not realize it is heavy, we will not put it down. Just so.

If we see that birth is suffering, then we stop all births. If we see aging, then we uproot rāga, lobha, dosa, moha — greed, hatred, delusion — along with all ambition, striving, and craving. Moreover, if we see sickness and disease — the extreme, miserable suffering, crying out in pain like this — if we see this, then we let go even more, we abandon even more. We abandon all upādāna, all clinging, thinking "this is mine, that is mine." Ultimately, our own self is not our self. There is only a site of pain, a site of ache — everywhere it's the same.

title: Ajahn Funn: When you’ve entered in and looked into the body on which you depend, in which you live, then enter in and look into…
content:
Place Your Mind in Buddho, Not in Children or Home or Work

When you’ve entered in and looked into the body on which you depend, in which you live, then enter in and look into your mind. How is your mind? This mind is what creates states of becoming and birth, creates kamma, creates animosity, creates dangers. This mind is what builds up evil, builds up bad kamma. So look at it. How does it build up evil and build up bad kamma? It’s voracious, frenzied, and restless. It wants that; it wants this. That’s how it is. It sends itself to the left, to the right, out in front, back behind, up, down. It can’t stay established right in the middle. So enter in and look into your mind.

Don’t place your mind anywhere else. Place it with Buddho, i.e., awareness itself. Wherever your awareness is located, focus your mind right there in Buddho, the awareness. Don’t place it anywhere else. If you focus it over there at this place or that, it’s going to suffer. Don’t place it with your children or grandchildren. Don’t place it with your home or your workplace. Place it right at your mind. Try to see how it’s functioning, what it has. Know and understand. If it starts any becoming or birth, try to see it.

title: Ajahn Funn: I want you to understand our practice of virtue. We gain happiness and prosperity because of virtue. Virtue means normalcy in body, normalcy…
content:
Virtue: Normalcy in Body and Mind, Abandoning Harm

I want you to understand our practice of virtue. We gain happiness and prosperity because of virtue. Virtue means normalcy in body, normalcy in mind. It’s a matter of abandoning harm, refraining from harm, great and small, through our body and mind. We don’t do anything evil, don’t engage in bad kamma. No matter what level of becoming we go to, we won’t be evil.

We’ve been born into the world and we complain of the suffering. We complain of difficulties, complain of poverty, complain of being in debt. We’ve studied well, we’ve gained a good education, but once we’ve completed our studies and started work, we still find that it’s difficult. Why? Because we haven’t made merit for many lifetimes. So even though we want status, we don’t gain it. Even though we want wealth, even though we want beauty, we don’t gain them.

title: Ajahn Funn: In whatever realm or birth we are, we have been born. From now on, know the place of abiding. When we sit in…
content:
When the Mind Is Peaceful, That Is Our Abiding Place

In whatever realm or birth we are, we have been born. From now on, know the place of abiding. When we sit in samādhi, we go to our own abiding place. When the mind is peaceful, it is easy in body and mind, not suffering, not hot, not chaotic, not turbulent – at ease. That is our abiding place. When our mind is like that, it brings happiness and prosperity, in the present and in the future. Such a mind must lead to a happy destiny (sugati), because right now it has happiness; when it ceases with the aggregates, it will also have happiness. If our mind is unwholesome, suffering, chaotic, drowsy, sleepy, suffering in body and mind, then such a mind leads to an unhappy destiny (dugati). If it is born as a human, it is a human with suffering, low, vile. If not human, it could be a peta, an animal, or a hell being. Therefore, let us all understand.

When we see these things as suffering and we do not want them, then let us all do buddho, buddho to dispel and drive them away. If asked: will we suffer if we do not want it? Who would want it? We must practice opanayiko – look and see: who sees suffering? It is not trees, mountains, or caves that suffer; not villages or cities that suffer; not roads that suffer. Our mind is the one that suffers.

title: Ajahn Funn: Right now, we don’t yet know. Whatever arises, we grasp that as self. Consequently, we get suffering and hardship. Now, whatever arises, we…
content:
Samādhi: The Mind Established Firmly as a Reliable Refuge

Right now, we don’t yet know. Whatever arises, we grasp that as self. Consequently, we get suffering and hardship. Now, whatever arises, we don’t grasp it, don’t concoct it, don’t fabricate it. We are still in ignorance (avijjā). When there is ignorance — delusion — then it goes about concocting, fabricating, grasping other things. When we have clear knowledge (vijjā), then we have clear knowing and true seeing: lokavidū — knower of the world. If we already know, how can it deceive us? We already know, already see; it cannot deceive us. We must not let the mind move away from its established foundation — that is, the state of knowing.

Samādhi is the mind that is established firmly, not wavering, shaking, or vacillating in the face of anything. Established firmly, like a sturdy hut here: anyone can come and take shelter in it. Even when wind, sun, or rain comes, they can take shelter. A refuge (saraṇa) must be reliable. Our mind is the same. When we say it’s unreliable, that means we want to stay here, but it goes and stays somewhere else. We want one place, it goes and takes another place — that’s unreliable. If you make it still, it can remain still. Then it can be relied upon, taken as a refuge. This is how we cut off demerit, kamma, enmity, and all dangers and unwholesome things, making them cease and be quenched.

title: Ajahn Funn: As for sīla-pāramī: people merely receive the precepts, they don't keep them. They think the precepts belong to the monks. If the monk…
content:
Sīla Is Born Together with Us: Two Legs, Two Arms, One Head – The Five Precepts

As for sīla-pāramī: people merely receive the precepts, they don't keep them. They think the precepts belong to the monks. If the monk doesn't give them, they think they haven't got the precepts. This is sīlabbata-parāmāsa (clinging to mere rites and rituals) – just caressing the precepts. In truth, our sīla is born together with us. The five precepts are complete from birth: two legs, two arms, one head – this itself is the five precepts. We received them from our mother. From birth they are already present. Since we have these five precepts pure in this way, we should preserve them. Guard our body, guard our speech, guard our mind properly. Do not commit any fault, great or small, by body, speech, or mind. What are the five faults? Pāṇātipātā – he tells us to abstain, not to do it. That is a fault, not a precept. Adinnādānā – that too is a fault, not a precept. Kāmesumicchācārā – that is not a precept, only a fault. Musāvādā – he tells us to abstain; it is a fault, not a precept. Surāmerayamajja – this too is only a fault. If we do not commit these five wrong actions, wherever we are we have sīla. At home in our room we have sīla. In the forest or jungle we have sīla. In a car or on a train we have sīla. Understand sīla in this way.

title: Ajahn Funn: If we don't arise, what will there be to age? If we don't age, what will there be to get sick? If we…
content:
Cutting the Current: Not Arising, Not Dying – Reaching the Deathless

If we don't arise, what will there be to age? If we don't age, what will there be to get sick? If we don't get sick, what will there be to die? If we don't die, what will there be to suffer? But we are born. Then we age. Then we get sick. Then we die. And after death, we are born again. Then age again, then sick again, then die again. We revolve in birth and death. The Buddha cut the current. He did not arise. Since he did not arise, he did not die. Not dying, he did not suffer. He reached the deathless (amataṁ). Now from here on, each of you listen on your own. Listen to your own heart – not to anything else. Make a mental note: whatever sounds you hear, know that they are not dangerous. You don't need to be upset. Let your mind be at ease, comfortable. Focus and look. Know here whether your mind is good or not good.

If our mind is good, everything we do is good. This is it. People blame this and that. They themselves are not good, yet they blame the country for not being good. They themselves are not peaceful, yet they blame the country for not being peaceful. If each person individually becomes peaceful, then the nation becomes peaceful.

title: Ajahn Funn: If the mind is not calm, it keeps creating kamma, creating enmity, creating danger. It never ends. Danger ends because our mind has…
content:
Danger Ends Because Our Mind Has No Danger – Kamma Ends Right There

If the mind is not calm, it keeps creating kamma, creating enmity, creating danger. It never ends. Danger ends because our mind has no danger. Kamma ends because our mind has no kamma. Evil ends because our mind has no evil. Suffering ends because our mind has no suffering. See? It ends right there. If our mind does not suffer, what can make it suffer? If our mind is not evil, where would evil come from? There is none.

From now on, each of you practice. Contemplate to know and see. This is what is called listening to Dhamma. All Dhamma – who makes it for us? No one makes it. We make it ourselves. Now we are living here in seclusion, in peace, free from dangers. Everything must be heard and seen. No one summons us to take anything. No one tells us to do anything at all. All evil kamma, all happiness and suffering, all good and bad – we are the ones who do them ourselves.

title: Ajahn Funn: In the Dhammacakkappavattanasutta (the first sermon), the Buddha taught: "Dve me, bhikkhave" — "Monks, you should not pursue two extremes." That is, love…
content:
The Two Extremes: Love and Hate – The Middle Way

In the Dhammacakkappavattanasutta (the first sermon), the Buddha taught: "Dve me, bhikkhave" — "Monks, you should not pursue two extremes." That is, love and hate. Practice the middle way (majjhimāpaṭipadā) — neither love nor hate. Because love, desire, and delight springing from lust are the fire of rāga. When this fire of rāga ignites within anyone's mind, it burns that person's mind, causing distress, struggling and writhing without peace, wandering under the power of love until they lose mindfulness, become insane, lack the wisdom and skillful means to protect themselves, lose restraint and caution, have no hiri (moral shame) and ottappa (moral dread) — no shame or fear of wrongdoing in their mind. They then engage in evil, unwholesome deeds that bring suffering and harm, that bring danger and mental distress upon themselves. This is the result of love and the fire of rāga. Monks, you should not pursue this one extreme — the side of love — which is suffering, harmful, and fraught with various dangers.
